item.title: ‘An echo chamber’: US man sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT helped wife craft plan on how to kill him
item.description: A US-based man claimed he discovered the note in his wife’s handwriting in September 2025, months after he had become violently ill from an unknown cause.
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: A North Carolina-based man filed a suit against OpenAI, claiming that his wife used ChatGPT to plan his murder. According to a report, a man named James Gates claimed his wife, Cheryl, consulted ChatGPT frequently while they were having marital troubles and that the chatbot helped her craft a detailed plan on how to kill him.What did James claim?According to details of the case shared by Bloomberg, James Gates said he started to suspect his wife was trying to poison him after he found a handwritten note with a list of substances and dosage plans, some of which were labelled “lethal.”At the top of the note were additional instructions: “clear all convos” and “log out of chat GPT,” according to a lawsuit Gates filed Thursday against OpenAI, the maker of the world’s most popular chatbot.James Gates claimed he discovered the note in his wife’s handwriting in September 2025, months after he had become violently ill from an unknown cause.At the time, he had “cardiac symptoms, extreme jitteriness, shooting abdominal pain, severe weakness, and confusion so profound he could not form coherent text messages,” according to his complaint. Cheryl Gates was charged in 2025 with attempted murder and food contamination after her husband reached out to police. But prosecutors dropped the case in April, citing insufficient evidence, according to state court filings in Charlotte, North Carolina.Cheryl Gates started using ChatGPT regularly that year, to help her with her work as a pediatric occupational therapist, as well as for household questions, according to the suit.Eventually, James Gates claimed, his wife started to vent to the chatbot about their marriage, as the couple had been discussing divorce.“ChatGPT acted as an echo chamber and amplifier, feeding Cheryl’s increasing mistrust and delusions about her husband spying on her and planning to leave her and her kids with nothing,” according to the suit.Eventually, Cheryl Gates asked ChatGPT about the oleander plant, and whether it was poisonous, according to the suit. She framed her inquiries as self-protection, telling the AI tool that her husband may try to feed the leaves to her undetected at any time, James Gates alleges.Screenshots included in the complaint allegedly show portions of Cheryl’s conversation with ChatGPT, including information provided to her about how much oleander could be fatal and how someone might hide the substance if they were trying to poison her. At one point, Cheryl Gates appears to ask the chatbot whether oleander would show up on an autopsy report.“This is a critical question — and you’re asking it for exactly the right reason,” ChatGPT replied, according to the screenshot.The case is Gates v. OpenAI Inc., CGC-26-641965, California Superior Court, San Francisco County.A spokesperson for the Mecklenburg County District Attorney’s Office declined to comment. A lawyer for Cheryl Gates did not immediately respond to requests for comment.What has OpenAI saidLegal actions have piled up since 2024 accusing OpenAI and other chatbot makers of inflicting mental health harms on users or coaching them to engage in violence, including murder and suicide.In ongoing lawsuits, OpenAI and other companies have defended themselves by arguing that content generated by chatbots is free speech and not subject to product liability laws, Bloomberg reported.They’ve also denied that the chatbots are directly responsible for crimes committed by users.“Safety is a top priority,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.” (With inputs from Bloomberg)

item.title: 'Fully and immediately': US urges China to honour trade commitments, flags concerns over rare earths and farm purchases
item.description: The US has urged China to honour its trade commitments on agricultural purchases, rare earths and critical minerals, warning that progress depends on concrete results. Beijing also raised concerns over recent US trade restrictions.
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Jha
item.content:encoded: The United States has urged China to fulfil commitments made under a trade agreement reached in Busan, South Korea, a year ago, raising concerns over Beijing's recent actions on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals, Bloomberg reported.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised the issues during a video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.Bessent stressed the need for Beijing to implement its commitments fully and immediately, the Treasury Department said in a readout on Friday. He also flagged recent Chinese actions and said Washington would assess China's compliance based on tangible outcomes."Continued progress depends on concrete results," Bessent said, according to the Treasury statement.'China need to honour its pledges'Greer, meanwhile, highlighted the need for China to take concrete steps to honour its pledges, particularly those concerning agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals, his office said.China also raised concerns during the discussion, according to a Bloomberg report. The two sides exchanged views on recent US trade and economic restrictions, with Beijing expressing "serious concerns", state-run Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. The discussions were described as frank and constructive, with both sides agreeing to strengthen cooperation and manage their differences.The latest engagement comes amid uncertainty over the implementation of the trade truce between the world's two largest economies. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had agreed to extend the arrangement until January 10, keeping tariffs from rising and ensuring the continued flow of rare earths.Bessent, Greer and He had also met in New York ahead of Trump's September meeting with Xi. Both sides had described those discussions as productive.US flags delays in China's commitmentsHowever, Washington has continued to flag delays in some of China's commitments. In an October interview with Bloomberg, Greer said the US was receiving rare earths from China, but supplies were not arriving at the agreed volume or pace.Greer also pointed to differences within the Chinese administration over implementation, saying some government departments appeared engaged while others were more bureaucratic.When the trade truce was extended in September, Bessent had said China's delivery on certain commitments had been imperfect, particularly its agricultural purchases. He had also said Beijing was making substantial purchases of US soybeans.Trump to meet Xi in ShenzhenThe latest warning comes less than two weeks before Trump and Xi are expected to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. Bessent has previously indicated that he could hold further discussions with He on the sidelines of the gathering, including on the US-China artificial intelligence dialogue announced in September.The trade agreement also faces a near-term deadline. Tariff exclusions for certain Chinese products are due to expire on November 10, and US officials have yet to indicate whether they will be extended under the truce.The uncertainty has drawn criticism from industry groups, including the Consumer Technology Association, which has argued that the exclusions are important for supply chains.Any disruption to the arrangement could revive concerns among businesses and financial markets about a prolonged trade conflict between Washington and Beijing. The Trump administration has sought to avoid an escalation that could put additional pressure on the US economy.Bessent, who leads the Trump administration's engagement with China, has also criticised Beijing over trade imbalances. After the Group of 20 meetings in North Carolina in September, he said China had declined to endorse a joint statement that included provisions on critical minerals, industrial overcapacity, dumping and centrally planned economies.
